title: Turing's Imaginary Machine
objective: After this level you can explain Alan Turing's 1936 idea of a simple machine reading a tape, and why it can compute anything computable.
summary: Turing's 1936 machine: a tape of squares, a head that reads, writes and moves one square at a time, and a finite rulebook. A universal machine runs any machine's rules from its tape.

cards.headline: In 1936 Alan Turing described a computer made of little more than a tape.
cards.body: It was an abstract machine, an idea on paper rather than a device to build. So why does a machine that never existed sit at the heart of computer science?

cards.headline: A tape, a head and a rulebook
cards.body: Picture a tape divided into squares, as long as you need, each blank or holding one symbol. A head sits over one square at a time. It can read the symbol there, write or erase one, and move one square left or right. At every moment the machine is in one of a limited number of states, and a finite table of instructions says what to do next. That's the whole machine.

cards.headline: One machine that can be any machine
cards.body: Turing's cleverest step was to write a machine's instructions onto the tape itself. His universal machine reads that description and then does whatever the described machine would do. Change what's on the tape, and the same machine does a different job.

mascot.line: Keep this: a program can be written down as data for another machine to read. Every computer since builds on that.

cards.fact: Everything humanly computable can be computed by a universal Turing machine.
cards.context: That claim is called the Church-Turing thesis. Strictly, it can't be proved, because it matches an everyday idea, what can be computed, to a precise definition. It's a thesis, not a theorem.

cards.headline: Turing's machine: imagined
learned: A tape of squares, a head and a rulebook
The head reads, writes and moves one square
A universal machine reads another's instructions
The Church-Turing thesis can't be proved

questions.prompt: Match each part of Turing's machine with its description.

pairs.right: Sits over one square at a time

questions.explanation: The tape is divided into squares, the head sits over one square at a time, and a finite table of instructions says what to do next.

questions.prompt: How can one universal Turing machine do the job of any other Turing machine?

options.label: It is taken apart and rebuilt by hand for every new job
options.rationale: Its point is that it never needs rebuilding.

options.label: It has an endless number of heads, one per job
options.rationale: It has one head, like any Turing machine.

options.label: It guesses the answer first, then checks it
options.rationale: It follows the described machine's instructions.

options.label: It reads the other machine's instructions from its tape

questions.explanation: The other machine's instructions are written on the tape, and the universal machine carries them out.

questions.prompt: Turing's machine checks its table of instructions before every step. For each instruction, a real processor repeats the _____ cycle.

options.label: read, write, erase, move
options.rationale: Those are a Turing machine head's actions, not a processor's cycle.

options.label: store, mill, print
options.rationale: Those echo Babbage's engine, not a processor's cycle.

questions.explanation: A processor fetches the instruction its program counter points to, decodes it and executes it.
